planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in spring after frost risk; Lila is a cold-hardy Mexican-race avocado cultivar suited to the northern edge of avocado growing range.

directions: Plant in full sun in very well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil; root rot in heavy, wet soils is the primary avocado killer and is not recoverable once established. Lila is a Mexican-race avocado cultivar valued for its combination of cold hardiness and rich, high-oil-content flesh with the classic anise-tinged flavor typical of Mexican-race avocados, distinguishing it from the milder Guatemalan and West Indian races. Mexican-race avocados tend to have thinner, smoother skin and smaller fruit than Guatemalan types, but generally offer superior cold tolerance, an important trait for gardeners at the northern edge of avocado range. Harvest based on typical days from flowering for the cultivar rather than skin color alone, and ripen indoors at room temperature after picking.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Cold-Hardy Avocado Cultivars
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Avocado Production in South Texas

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in spring after frost risk; Poncho is a cold-hardy Texas-selected Mexican-race avocado cultivar.

directions: Plant in full sun in very well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil; root rot in heavy, wet soils is the primary avocado killer and is not recoverable once established. Poncho is one of several Texas-selected Mexican-race avocado cultivars bred and trialed for cold hardiness at the northern limit of where avocados can survive outdoors, bearing medium fruit with rich, high-oil flesh and the anise-tinged flavor typical of Mexican-race types. Its selection reflects decades of Texas home-gardener efforts to identify avocado seedlings that survive occasional hard freezes with only minor damage. Harvest based on typical days from flowering for the cultivar rather than skin color alone, and ripen indoors at room temperature after picking.
sources: Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Avocado Production in South Texas
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Cold-Hardy Avocado Cultivars

common_name: Del Rio Avocado (Cold-Hardy Texas Mexican-Type Avocado)

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in spring after frost risk; Del Rio is a cold-hardy Texas Mexican-race avocado cultivar named for the border city where it originated or was extensively trialed.

directions: Plant in full sun in very well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil; root rot in heavy, wet soils is the primary avocado killer and is not recoverable once established. Del Rio is a Mexican-race avocado cultivar selected for cold hardiness in South and West Texas, where hard freezes regularly test the limits of what avocado trees can survive, bearing medium fruit with rich, high-oil flesh and the anise-tinged flavor typical of Mexican-race types. It represents the ongoing regional effort among Texas home orchardists to identify and propagate avocado selections tough enough for zone 8b-9a gardens. Harvest based on typical days from flowering for the cultivar rather than skin color alone, and ripen indoors at room temperature after picking.
sources: Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Avocado Production in South Texas
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Cold-Hardy Avocado Cultivars

planting.note: Plant container-grown, grafted trees in spring after all frost danger has passed in full sun; Glenn is a compact, precocious Florida mango cultivar that fits smaller dooryard plantings and large containers.

directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile soil, protecting young trees from any frost since mangoes have no cold tolerance. Glenn is a Florida-bred mango cultivar prized for its comparatively compact, semi-dwarf growth habit and precocious bearing, producing medium-to-large fruit with yellow-blushed skin and smooth, fiberless, sweet flesh with a mild, non-resinous flavor that makes it broadly popular for fresh eating. Its smaller stature compared to many mango cultivars suits large containers or smaller yards where a full-size mango tree would be impractical. Reduce watering as fruit approaches ripeness to concentrate flavor, and harvest when fruit gives slightly to gentle pressure and develops full color.
